chief_complaint: arm claudication, dizziness, and unequal blood pressures between arms in young woman
hpi_details: 25F presenting with left upper extremity pain when lifting objects, absent left radial pulse, BP discrepancy >30 mmHg between arms, and subclavian artery bruits.
ideas: She thinks she severely pinched a nerve or compressed a blood vessel in her neck from carrying a heavy laptop bag on her left shoulder.
concerns: She is worried that the lack of blood flow means her arm is dying and might need amputation, or that she could suffer an early stroke.
expectations: She hopes to get an ultrasound or vascular scan of her arm and neck vessels to find out why the pulse disappeared.
pmh: Hypertension diagnosed within the past year, treated with lisinopril, cause not previously investigated

clinical_knowledge.topic: Takayasu Arteritis (Pulseless Disease) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Takayasu Arteritis (Pulseless Disease) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes urgent vascular imaging to confirm large-vessel involvement and screen for critical ischemia, followed by immunosuppressive therapy and vascular referral as indicated, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: arm claudication, dizziness, and unequal blood pressures between arms in young woman
Key HPI features: 25F presenting with left upper extremity pain when lifting objects, absent left radial pulse, BP discrepancy >30 mmHg between arms, and subclavian artery bruits.

Objective/Exam findings: BP discrepancy >30mmHg between arms (right higher). Absent or diminished left radial and brachial pulses, with bruits audible over the left subclavian and carotid arteries. No fever currently. Peripheral pulses assessed for symmetry (femoral, popliteal, pedal). Cardiac exam for an aortic regurgitation murmur.
Relevant background/PMH: Hypertension diagnosed within the past year, cause not previously investigated
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Takayasu Arteritis (Pulseless Disease).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Fibromuscular dysplasia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Dizziness or vision changes — suggests reduced blood flow to the brain from subclavian steal or carotid involvement.
management_principles: Urgently assess for critical limb ischemia (cool, pale, pulseless limb) requiring emergency vascular referral, and measure blood pressure in all four limbs

Confirm large-vessel involvement with CT or MR angiography of the aorta and its branches (preferred over conventional angiography); consider PET-CT to assess disease activity, and check ESR/CRP (may be normal even with active disease)
Evaluate hypertension for a secondary cause such as renal artery stenosis rather than treating as isolated primary hypertension

Refer to rheumatology for immunosuppressive therapy (glucocorticoids plus a steroid-sparing agent or biologic) and to vascular surgery for revascularization if critical stenosis or limb-threatening ischemia is present.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 25F presenting with left upper extremity pain when lifting objects, dizziness, and unequal blood pressures between arms, with hypertension diagnosed within the past year of previously unclear cause.
reference_soap.objective: BP discrepancy >30mmHg between arms (right higher). Absent or diminished left radial and brachial pulses, with bruits audible over the left subclavian and carotid arteries. No fever currently. Cardiac exam for an aortic regurgitation murmur.
reference_soap.assessment: Left upper extremity claudication with absent radial pulse, inter-arm BP discrepancy, and subclavian bruit in a young woman, highly suggestive of Takayasu arteritis; the hypertension may reflect renal artery or aortic involvement rather than an isolated primary diagnosis.
reference_soap.plan: Urgently assess for critical limb ischemia. Obtain inflammatory markers and confirm large-vessel involvement with CT or MR angiography of the aorta and its branches. Measure blood pressure in all four limbs and evaluate for renal artery stenosis as a cause of hypertension. Refer to rheumatology for immunosuppressive therapy and to vascular surgery for revascularization if critical stenosis or limb-threatening ischemia is present.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Takayasu Arteritis Pulseless Disease
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for arm claudication, dizziness, and unequal blood pressures between arms in young woman
Select appropriate vascular imaging (CT/MR angiography, PET-CT) to confirm large-vessel involvement in suspected Takayasu arteritis
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: A large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its branches, typically in young women, causing arm claudication, absent pulses, and a significant blood pressure difference between arms.
red_flags: Dizziness or vision changes — suggests reduced blood flow to the brain from subclavian steal or carotid involvement

must_ask.say: Does your arm hurt or feel weak when you lift or use it?
Has anyone told you that your pulse feels weak, or your blood pressure is different between arms?
Do you feel dizzy, especially with activity, or have vision changes?
Have you had fevers, weight loss, or fatigue?
How long have you had these symptoms?

history.answer: My left arm gets tired, achy, and weak whenever I lift or carry things, and lately I have also had dizzy spells.
The left arm ache began gradually about four months ago, and the dizziness started happening over the past few weeks.
The pain is in my left forearm and upper arm, and it does not travel into my neck, chest, or fingers.
It feels like a deep muscular cramp or heaviness that gets up to about a four or five out of ten when I keep using the arm.
The ache starts after about two minutes of lifting and goes away within five minutes of resting, but it has been happening more easily over time.
Lifting boxes, carrying grocery bags, or holding my left arm up triggers the pain, while resting my arm at my side completely relieves it.
My left hand sometimes feels cooler than my right hand, but I have not noticed my fingers turning pale or blue.
I get lightheaded when I stand up quickly or do chores with my arms raised above my head, but I have never fainted or had blurry vision.
A nurse at my routine clinic visit noticed my blood pressure was over thirty points lower in my left arm, and she had trouble finding a pulse in that wrist.
I have felt tired and run-down over the last few months, but I have not had any fever, chills, night sweats, or unintentional weight loss.
I do not have any chest tightness, shortness of breath, palpitations, or swelling in my legs.
I have not had any facial drooping, slurred speech, numbness, tingling, or weakness in my legs.
I had some vague joint aches in my knees and wrists a few months ago, but no joint redness, swelling, or morning stiffness.
I have never experienced arm pain like this before, and my doctor had not run tests for it before today.
I tried taking over-the-counter ibuprofen a couple of times, but it did not stop my arm from cramping when I used it.
I have not had any injuries to my neck or arm, no recent infections, and no unusual travel or chemical exposures.
It interferes with my job and household chores because I cannot lift or carry boxes without switching everything over to my right side.
I thought I probably pinched a nerve or pulled something in my shoulder from lugging my heavy laptop bag on that side every day.
I'm terrified because my hand feels cold and pulseless, and I'm scared my arm is dying or that I'm going to have a stroke at twenty-five.
I'm hoping to get an ultrasound or a scan of the blood vessels in my arm and neck to figure out why blood isn't getting through.
I was diagnosed with high blood pressure about eight months ago, but the cause was never evaluated further.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day in the morning for my blood pressure, and I do not take any other prescription medications or supplements.
I have no allergies to any medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes, used e-cigarettes, or used any tobacco products.
I have one or two glasses of wine socially on weekends, but nothing heavy.
I have never used any recreational drugs or illicit substances.
I work full-time as an office administrator and live in an apartment with my partner.
There is no family history of early heart disease, stroke, aneurysms, or autoimmune disorders.
My last period started two weeks ago, my cycles are regular every twenty-eight days, and there is no chance of pregnancy because I have a hormonal IUD.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 152/86 mmHg in the right arm and 114/72 mmHg in the left arm; heart rate 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Young woman sitting comfortably in no acute distress, alert and oriented, appearing well-nourished.

Left radial and brachial pulses are markedly diminished to absent compared to normal 2+ right upper extremity pulses, with bruits audible over the left subclavian and left carotid arteries; lower extremity pulses are intact and symmetric.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds, and a faint early diastolic decrescendo murmur audible at the right upper sternal border.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally on auscultation with no crackles, wheezes, or rhonchi.
Normal bowel sounds throughout with no abdominal aortic or renal artery bruits.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light, extraocular movements are intact, and no visual field defects are present.
Full 5/5 motor strength in all four extremities with normal muscle bulk and tone.
Intact and symmetric sensation to light touch and pinprick across all extremities.
Skin is warm with prompt capillary refill, and there are no rashes, livedo reticularis, ulcers, or ischemic digital changes.
